newsitem.title: UK: BOXING-BRITISH WOMEN FIGHT FOR EQUAL RIGHTS.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-BRITISH WOMEN FIGHT FOR EQUAL RIGHTS.

text.p: Muscles rippling and long chestnut curls beaded with sweat, former wild-child Jane Couch is frighteningly ruthless inside the boxing ring.

Outside the arena, the women's world welterweight champion is no less aggressive, passionately arguing her case for the right to fight professionally in Britain and earn the same money as her male contemporaries.

But the feisty 28-year-old and her fellow women boxers, viewed as a freakish compromise between mud-wrestlers and gladiators, have yet to convince British authorities or the general public to take them seriously.
"I love boxing because it's controversial," Couch said in an interview. "I love getting in there and proving I can do it better than a man."
Male boxers can rake in $5 million for a single fight; Couch is lucky to get $10,000 for a match in the United States. And she can't earn a penny fighting in Britain.
Women boxers say interest in their sport is growing and they are ready to fight the authorities for equal rights in the sport.
"We want these organisations to realise that they are totally unfounded in discriminating against women's boxing," said Couch's manager Tex Woodward.
"Provided it's properly supervised and controlled, women should be able to have the same freedom as men."
The Women's International Boxing Federation (WIBF) says it plans to challenge the British authorities this year, although refusing to specify exactly what action they have in mind.
"It's time to challenge the 'old boys'," said WIBF spokesman Jimmy Finn.
Although women's boxing is no longer illegal in Britain, authorities refuse to recognise it as a professional sport on the grounds that it is unsafe.
Supporters of women's boxing say the issue is not whether the sport is dangerous but whether there is any justification for what they say is blatant sexual discrimination.
"The current situation is despicable," said Couch's lawyer Andrew Brecher. "If men are allowed to box and earn so much money then why aren't women? It's discriminatory and it's patronising."
Lancashire-born Couch, who shot to the top of her profession after just two years, is a trail-blazer for would-be women boxers in Britain, and has generated a whirlwind of media attention.
She hopes the media spotlight will help dispel some of the myths surrounding women in the ring and spur the British Board of Boxing Control to rethink its rules.

"The average British attitude is way behind the rest of the world, but it's got to change," said Couch. "It's one of the fastest growing sports around, so it's only a matter of time before women boxers have the same status as men."
Britain's other world champion, Cheryl Robertson, echoes Couch's frustration.

"It's a disgusting situation. It makes me really angry," said the world bantamweight champion. "If I applied for a licence to box professionally I'd be turned down purely because I'm a woman. It just isn't fair."

Robertson, who successfully combines her sport with bringing up two young children and pursuing a career, said she was tired of people regarding women boxers as freaks and wished they would start giving them the respect they deserved.
"When people put me down, I ask them if they have ever seen me fight," said Robertson. "We train hard and we fight just as well as men."

While Britain's women boxers have yet to gain the stature of their counterparts in the United States and in other European countries, experts say they expect the number of women boxers in Britain to grow from fewer than 100 to around 500 over the next three years.
That expansion could be helped by a decision from the Amateur Boxing Association (ABA) to allow girls as young as 11 to box in amateur bouts from October.
Couch, whose early street brawls often landed her in police cells, bubbles with enthusiasm about the move, which should ensure safer training for women boxers.
"I'm not saying boxing's a safe sport, because no sport is safe," she said, "but it's much less dangerous if it's out in the open and properly supervised."
Finn said safety was a priority for the WIBF, and they took great care over medical tests.
However, attracting much-needed investment to develop shields to protect the lower abdomen and breast areas was a real problem, he added.
The idea of women donning boxing gloves remains highly emotional, even in the United States where a women's boxing championship was recently broadcast live for the first time.
Ostracised by male-dominated training gyms, and jeered at by the public for stepping outside the feminine steretype, novice women boxers are finding it hard to break through the barriers in Britain.

Finn said while many practised boxaerobics, kick-boxing and training with punch bags, few went on to proper fights because trainers and promoters feared they would lose their licenses if they took on women.
"My gym is buzzing with competent women boxers," said the owner of one London gymnasium. "But none of them are about to put on gumshields and fight."
Couch said she was planning a United Kingdom roadshow to coincide with the lifting of the ABA's 116-year-old age restriction which she hopes will encourage more women into the ring.

Having broken away from her own background of drugs, alcohol abuse and backstreet fights, Couch hopes she can convince other young tearaways to redirect their natural aggression into a professional fighting career.
